clinicalPearls: Most herniations occur posterolaterally at L4/5 and L5/S1, compressing the traversing nerve root and producing dermatomal leg pain (sciatica)
Leg pain typically exceeds back pain and follows a dermatomal distribution: L5 to the dorsum of the foot and great toe, S1 to the sole and lateral foot
The straight-leg-raise (Lasegue) test reproduces radicular pain within roughly 30 to 70 degrees of elevation, and a positive crossed straight-leg-raise is highly specific
Motor, reflex, and sensory findings localise the level: an absent ankle jerk suggests S1, while weak great-toe dorsiflexion suggests L5
Symptoms are typically aggravated by sitting, coughing, sneezing, or the Valsalva manoeuvre
The natural history is largely favourable, with most radiculopathy settling within weeks to a few months as the herniation resorbs, so initial management is conservative
MRI is reserved for persistent, severe, or progressive symptoms or when injection or surgery is contemplated, because asymptomatic disc bulges are common
Management includes analgesia, activity modification, physiotherapy, and nerve-root or epidural injection; discectomy is considered for refractory pain or significant neurological deficit
reference.pathophysiology: A lumbar disc herniation occurs when the gelatinous nucleus pulposus displaces through a tear or weakness in the surrounding annulus fibrosus. The displaced material, together with accompanying inflammatory mediators, irritates and compresses the adjacent nerve root, causing radicular pain and dermatomal sensory, motor, or reflex changes. Posterolateral herniations most often affect the traversing root at that level, whereas far-lateral (foraminal) herniations tend to compress the exiting root. Chemical radiculitis from inflammatory cytokines can generate pain even without marked mechanical compression, and gradual resorption of extruded disc material underlies the frequently favourable natural course.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Facet joint or sacroiliac joint referred pain
Piriformis syndrome or extraspinal sciatic nerve entrapment
Spinal tumour or infection when red flags are present
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the lumbar spine when symptoms are severe, persistent, or progressive
Plain radiographs to assess alignment and exclude other bony pathology
Nerve conduction studies and EMG in equivocal cases or to exclude peripheral neuropathy
CT or CT myelography where MRI is contraindicated
Targeted diagnostic selective nerve-root block to confirm the symptomatic level
redFlags: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or bilateral sciatica indicating possible cauda equina syndrome and mandating urgent MRI
Progressive or severe motor weakness such as a foot drop
Constitutional symptoms suggesting malignancy or infection
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally excellent: the majority of patients improve substantially within six to twelve weeks with conservative care, and surgery for persistent radiculopathy provides faster relief of leg pain, although longer-term outcomes often converge with non-operative treatment.
pitfalls: Rushing to image or operate on radiculopathy that would resolve spontaneously
Missing an evolving cauda equina syndrome by not asking about bladder, bowel, and saddle symptoms
Over-attributing symptoms to an incidental disc bulge seen on MRI
Overlooking a far-lateral herniation that compresses the exiting rather than the traversing root
references: NICE guideline: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s
management: Manage most cases conservatively, given the favourable natural history, with reassurance, continued activity, simple analgesia and NSAIDs, and physiotherapy
Add neuropathic pain agents such as amitriptyline or gabapentinoids for radicular pain where simple analgesia is insufficient
Offer a fluoroscopically guided epidural or transforaminal corticosteroid injection for persistent radicular pain not settling with conservative care
Reserve surgical microdiscectomy for radiculopathy that is severe, fails to improve over weeks to months, or is accompanied by a progressive neurological deficit
Recognise cauda equina syndrome as a surgical emergency requiring urgent MRI and immediate decompression
Investigate with MRI when symptoms are severe, persistent or progressive, correlating imaging with the clinical level
Refer to spinal surgery for progressive weakness, intractable pain or diagnostic uncertainty
